trajectory_summary: The call opens with a cost objection that the rep handles competently, briefly builds toward genuine interest and a vulnerability disclosure, then collapses the moment the customer's stated credit score comes in under 670. The rep takes the self-reported, from-memory-turned-live-pulled numbers at face value and ends the call with no alternative financing conversation or specialist handoff, closing a lead that had shown real engagement.
outcome_dispute: v1 outcome is unstated but the call functionally ends in a credit-based DQ; per qualifiers.credit_qualifier this is schema-correct IF setters are meant to DQ on stated credit. Two distinct issues complicate that read for this specific call: first, the customer read live scores off her own credit-monitoring app during the call (TransUnion 650, Equifax 633) rather than reciting a stale/remembered number, which is materially more reliable than the guess-based scenario Spencer's operator note describes — but it is still not the bureau pull Ion's own closer/lender would run, and three-bureau spread plus scoring-model differences (FICO vs the app's model) mean the actual pulled score could land above or below 670. Second, and separately, the customer herself flagged a specific accuracy problem on that same report — an incorrect delinquency mark ('I've got on here that I've been delinquent on two payments, and I haven't been delinquent on any payments for over two years') and an unexplained score drop from 705 to 633 with no reported change in her file. That disputed-accuracy claim is an independent reason the stated number may not reflect her true creditworthiness, on top of the general self-report-vs-bureau-pull gap. Per qualifiers.credit_qualifier's own policy_question_for_kenny, whether the setter should hard-DQ on a stated (even app-sourced) number or pass every lead to the closer's actual pull is unresolved — this call is a concrete example of that ambiguity costing a lead who was otherwise engaged and disclosed real financial pressure.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: credit-score DQ handling on a disputed/self-checked number
primary_coaching_focus.quote: Because you have to have a credit score over 670 to qualify for the program.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The customer explicitly told the rep her credit report has an inaccuracy (a delinquency mark she disputes) and an unexplained score drop, live on the call, immediately before the rep applied a hard cutoff to that same number and let her walk. Per the schema's own open policy_question_for_kenny, it's unresolved whether setters should DQ on stated credit at all — but even under a strict-DQ policy, the rep never acknowledged her dispute or offered a concrete re-check timeline, which is a coachable gap independent of that policy question.

key_moments.quote: Yeah. I just saved a $219 power bill this month and $3,331 power bill last month.
key_moments.stewart_read: Customer volunteers a bill figure unprompted in the opening seconds. Note the numbers here ($219 / $3,331) don't reconcile cleanly with the figures she gives later at 02:44 ($304, $506, roughly $1,000 across three-to-four months) — this is likely transcription/diarization noise on fast speech rather than two separate real bills, so the rep should not anchor hard on either specific figure without a bill-in-hand confirmation.

key_moments.stewart_read: Rather than flipping the bill she just gave him into an emotional hook (their-bill-vs-ours framing), the rep explains the mechanism of the program generically. This is a missed flip opportunity right after she supplied a bill number.
